section_summary: This section centers on Japan’s postwar population growth, economic resources, public health system, and the promotion of birth control as a means of avoiding hardship and renewed expansionism. It contains a 1945 appeal to General Douglas MacArthur, Warren S. Thompson’s extensive 1949 population-policy report and related correspondence, a newspaper defense of his proposals, and State Department memoranda circulating and evaluating his work. A largely unrelated 1946 Panama Desk routing slip closes the section.

subfiles.title: Letter urging General MacArthur to promote birth control in Japan
subfiles.about: Vickers urges MacArthur to teach and facilitate birth control as a means of reducing Japanese population pressure and preventing future wars.
subfiles.summary: Vickers argues that Japan’s militarism arose primarily from population pressure and the need for food rather than from hereditary national characteristics. Comparing Japan with the Netherlands, China, and India, he maintains that family limitation would improve living standards and reduce the impulse toward territorial expansion. He calls on MacArthur to undertake a courageous program of birth-control education.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding “A Population Policy for Japan”
subfiles.about: West sends Butterworth a copy of Warren S. Thompson’s report on population policy in Japan.
subfiles.summary: West identifies Thompson as a Miami University population expert and says that he found the enclosed report interesting. He forwards it to Butterworth for possible review by the State Department’s Far Eastern Affairs office.

subfiles.title: Draft letter forwarding Thompson’s supplementary views
subfiles.about: Butterworth prepares to send West a copy of Thompson’s response to State Department questions about Japanese birth control.
subfiles.summary: The draft recalls West’s earlier transmission of Thompson’s report. Butterworth explains that a member of his staff subsequently asked Thompson for further views and describes the resulting letter as worth reading. A cleaner final version appears on page 39.

subfiles.title: Thompson letter on the prospects for birth control in Japan, first copy
subfiles.about: Thompson evaluates whether Japanese birth control could spread rapidly enough to reduce postwar population growth.
subfiles.summary: Thompson acknowledges that Western experience suggests family limitation normally spreads over decades, but argues that Japan’s unusually low death rate, extensive health-center network, midwives, mass media, and public interest could accelerate the process. He nevertheless warns that Japan is already severely overpopulated and could face hardship, disorder, and renewed expansionism when American economic support ends. He recommends research into attitudes among different social classes while emphasizing that his optimism remains conditional.

subfiles.title: A Population Policy for Japan
subfiles.to: Chief of the occupation section to which Thompson was attached
subfiles.about: The report assesses Japan’s population-resource imbalance and argues for an explicit policy encouraging a lower birth rate.
subfiles.summary: Thompson surveys Japan’s limited agricultural and mineral resources, damaged industrial base, dependence on imports, and uncertain prospects for earning sufficient foreign exchange through textiles, machinery, and other exports. He argues that higher production and emigration cannot by themselves solve overpopulation and may actually encourage further growth when birth rates remain high. The report concludes that reducing the birth rate is the only durable way to balance population and resources, improve living standards, and diminish incentives for renewed military expansion. It urges American authorities to provide information and advice while leaving voluntary decisions to the Japanese people under their new democratic institutions.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 400: Japanese Population Problem
subfiles.from: Office of the United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Tokyo political adviser’s office transmits Thompson’s Nippon Times letter in response to reporting about Soviet criticism of his population proposals.
subfiles.summary: The despatch refers to an American Embassy Moscow telegram concerning an Izvestiya article about Thompson’s letter. It encloses the May 7 Nippon Times text and explains that Thompson had served as an adviser to SCAP on population problems. It also identifies Kaschmitter’s Catholic news publication as the target of Thompson’s response.

subfiles.title: “Raps Birth Control Critic: Dr. Thompson Insists His Proposal Is the Only Answer to Overpopulation Here”
subfiles.about: Thompson rebuts Father William S. Kaschmitter’s interpretation of his views and defends birth control as the only permanent solution to Japan’s overpopulation.
subfiles.summary: Thompson clarifies that although he favors opening unused lands to crowded populations, emigration cannot provide Japan with prompt or lasting relief. He emphasizes the logistical impossibility of moving people as fast as Japan’s population was increasing and argues that migration without a falling birth rate would be futile. He concludes that Japan’s public-health organization and publicity channels could spread effective family limitation more rapidly than Western precedent might suggest.

subfiles.title: Thompson letter on the prospects for birth control in Japan, signed copy
subfiles.about: A clean signed copy of Thompson’s assessment of the practical prospects for rapid birth-control adoption in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Thompson identifies Japan’s low death rate, more than 700 model health centers, widespread use of midwives, active press discussion, and government approval as reasons family limitation might spread unusually quickly. He cautions that neither official statements nor public interest prove that families will actually adopt the methods. He also warns that Japan’s existing overpopulation and eventual loss of American subsidies could produce severe hardship, political disorder, and pressure for renewed aggression.

subfiles.title: Memorandum requesting Economic Affairs comments
subfiles.to: Mr. Hamilton and the Office of Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Smith asks Economic Affairs whether it has comments on the population paper or subject for transmission to Mr. Rusk.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes that Rusk had not yet read the Far Eastern Affairs memorandum. It routes the matter through Hamilton and Assistant Secretary for Economic Affairs Thorp for possible substantive comment.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Japanese Population Problem
subfiles.to: W. Walton Butterworth, Mr. Allison, and Mr. Hamilton
subfiles.about: Fearey summarizes Thompson’s report, his own follow-up inquiry, and Thompson’s reply about mass adoption of birth control.
subfiles.summary: Fearey praises Thompson’s study as an excellent analysis of Japan’s population problem and economic prospects, noting that it helped inform an Economist article. He explains that he asked whether ordinary Japanese would use birth control enough to affect population growth if information and equipment were made inexpensive or free. He recommends that the recipients read Thompson’s reply because it contains several important points.

subfiles.title: Letter asking Thompson about mass adoption of birth control
subfiles.about: Fearey asks whether Japanese workers and farmers would practice birth control widely enough to affect population growth.
subfiles.summary: Fearey says he has read Thompson’s report with great interest but questions whether the Japanese masses would use contraceptive methods even if knowledge and equipment were readily available. He asks for foreign precedents involving rapidly expanding, low-income populations and contrasts educated Japanese with poorer farming and working classes. He describes the population problem as fundamental to Japan’s economic, political, and social difficulties.

subfiles.title: Memorandum transmitting a draft letter to West
subfiles.about: Fearey sends Butterworth the requested draft letter to Robert West enclosing Thompson’s response.
subfiles.summary: The brief memorandum states that the requested letter to West is attached. That letter was intended to pass Thompson’s supplementary discussion of Japanese population policy back to the Department of the Army.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding Thompson’s reply to Robert West
subfiles.about: Butterworth sends West a copy of Thompson’s supplementary letter on Japanese population policy.
subfiles.summary: Butterworth recalls that West had sent the State Department Thompson’s study the previous May. He explains that a staff member requested Thompson’s views on additional points and says the reply is sufficiently interesting to merit West’s attention. The Thompson letter reproduced on the following pages is the enclosure.

subfiles.title: Thompson letter on the prospects for birth control in Japan, enclosure copy
subfiles.about: This enclosure copy repeats Thompson’s analysis of the likelihood and consequences of rapid birth-control adoption in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Thompson argues that Japan’s public-health network, midwives, media attention, and official support could allow contraceptive knowledge to reach poorer families much faster than it did in the West. He discusses uncertainty about Premier Yoshida’s commitment, public sincerity, and resistance from expansionists, while noting reports of experimental hormonal contraception. He closes by warning that existing overpopulation and the withdrawal of American economic support could bring hunger, epidemics, political disorder, and renewed pressure for military expansion.

subfiles.title: DC/R routing slip from the Panama Desk
subfiles.to: Internal Department of State distribution offices
subfiles.about: The slip routes a record bearing the reference 894.202/9/7-2246 through several internal offices.
subfiles.summary: This is an administrative routing sheet rather than a substantive document on Japanese public health or population. It records action and copy-distribution codes, with a later notation dated July 30, and appears to have been filed here as a cross-reference or stray sheet.
